Alexander VI. Born Rodrigo Borgia, he reigned as pope from 1492 to 1503 and is remembered as the most notorious of the Renaissance popes, with a pontificate defined by corruption, nepotism, and political intrigue. A skilled diplomat and patron of the arts, he used the wealth of the papacy to advance the careers of his children, Cesare and Lucrezia Borgia.

In 1493, he issued the papal bull Inter Caetera, which established the Line of Demarcation that divided the non-Christian world between Spain and Portugal. This paved the way for the Treaty of Tordesillas. He promoted his illegitimate children Cesare and Lucrezia, using Cesare to militarily conquer the Romagna region and arranging marriages for Lucrezia to secure political alliances. In 1498, he ordered the excommunication and execution of Girolamo Savonarola, the reformist Dominican friar who had criticized his corruption and ruled Florence.

He won the papacy through simony—bribery—during the 1492 conclave, defeating his chief rival Giuliano della Rovere, who would later become Pope Julius II. He commissioned the Umbrian artist Pinturicchio to paint the elaborate frescoes of the Borgia Apartments in the Apostolic Palace. His reign became a symbol of the spiritual decay that eventually sparked the Protestant Reformation.
